a16z-20261020-c6ca3840.title: What Happens When Everyone Has a Health Expert in Their Pocket? | OpenAI’s Karan Singhal
a16z-20261020-c6ca3840.notes: More than 300 million people use ChatGPT for health and wellness questions each week. OpenAI’s Karan Singhal thinks that’s only the beginning: the longer-term goal is AI that can help people navigate their health proactively, while making trustworthy medical intelligence dramatically more accessible. Karan joins a16z Partner Jay Rughani to explain why OpenAI trains healthcare expertise directly into its general-purpose frontier models, how it works with hundreds of medical experts to evaluate safety and disagreement, and why the company sees AI as a complement to doctors rather than a replacement for medical care. They also discuss integrations with Epic, AI copilots for clinicians, and what happens as personal agents begin navigating appointments, health records, and other fragmented parts of the healthcare system. Looking further ahead, Karan makes the case that the cost of medical intelligence could continue to fall dramatically, allowing AI to act as a safety net for patients and clinicians, surface insights from years of health data, and potentially accelerate the discovery and validation of new treatments. a16z-20261018-ad389920.title: Why Real-World AI Is Harder Than the Benchmark | EliseAI’s Mario Martone
a16z-20261018-ad389920.notes: What changes when an AI mistake doesn’t just hurt a benchmark score, but affects someone’s housing or healthcare? EliseAI Head of Applied Research Mario Martone argues that deploying AI in essential industries requires a very different standard of reliability. Mario joins MTS to explain how EliseAI handles roughly 5 million phone calls a month, why LLMs aren’t the right solution for every problem, and how the team combines language models, traditional machine learning, neural networks, and internally built evaluations to decide what actually works in production.  Drawing on 15 years studying theoretical physics, Mario also explains how the scientific method shapes EliseAI’s research culture, from testing new models against its own benchmarks to fine-tuning open-source models and automating increasingly complex workflows across housing and healthcare. And he makes the case that applying AI to the real world can produce problems every bit as intellectually difficult as the ones he encountered studying string theory. a16z-20261014-e154dc9f.title: Can Open Models Keep Up With the AI Frontier? | Nathan Lambert
a16z-20261014-e154dc9f.notes: a16z Partner Lisha Li sits down with AI researcher and Trillium founder Nathan Lambert to ask how durable the gap really is between frontier AI labs and open models. Nathan argues that OpenAI and Anthropic have structural advantages in compute, capital, and the ability to pioneer new training paradigms, but open-model labs, particularly in China, have proven remarkably capable of following close behind. They unpack how much of that comes from distillation versus technical talent, why compute remains a major constraint, and how data, RL environments, and post-training are increasingly shaping model progress.  They also discuss Nathan’s new nonprofit research lab, Trillium, and its plans to open up parts of AI research that are increasingly difficult to study from the outside. That includes releasing RL environments and documenting how AI is actually being used to automate AI research, with the goal of demystifying recursive self-improvement and giving researchers and policymakers a clearer picture of what frontier systems can and cannot do. a16z-20261021-f2e0e7d5.title: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agents: Documents | Reducto’s Adit Abraham
a16z-20261021-f2e0e7d5.notes: AI agents can reason over enormous amounts of information, but much of the world’s actual work is still trapped in PDFs, spreadsheets, scans, and other formats that models struggle to reliably understand. Reducto co-founder and CEO Adit Abraham argues that solving this document layer is essential if agents are going to take on consequential work in healthcare, legal, finance, and insurance. Adit joins a16z General Partner Jennifer Li to explain why traditional OCR breaks down on messy real-world documents, how Reducto combines vision-language models with specialized infrastructure to reach high accuracy without sacrificing cost or latency, and why frontier models can silently drop information on long extraction tasks. Reducto now processes billions of pages each month, including its seven billionth page the morning of the recording.  They also discuss Reducto’s R1 model, agents that can review and correct their own document extraction, and the company’s push beyond simply reading files toward letting agents reliably work with and edit them. Underneath it all is a higher-stakes problem: when a misread word can affect a healthcare claim or financial decision, getting the input right matters just as much as making the model smarter. a16z-20261026-d59a34d0.title: OpenAI: When AI Agents Use Computers Faster Than You
a16z-20261026-d59a34d0.notes: AI agents are approaching a point where they can use computers faster than expert humans, turning the user interface itself into a universal way for AI to interact with software. OpenAI’s Ari Weinstein and James Sun argue that computer use is now entering its scaling moment, as better models, faster execution, and stronger safety controls make agents practical for more consumer and enterprise work. Ari and James join a16z’s Seema Amble and Fabrizio Serafini to explain how computer-using agents are already navigating legacy ERPs, reconciling financial data, handling procurement, and operating software without APIs or custom integrations. They also discuss why the harness around the model can matter as much as model intelligence, how enterprises can set deterministic guardrails around agent behavior, and why computer use could simultaneously extend the life of legacy software and accelerate the arrival of new AI-native applications.  Looking ahead, they make the case for a more proactive and fluid relationship with computers, where agents work in the background, collaborate with users in real time, and increasingly adapt to us rather than requiring us to learn how to use them. adhoc-20261029-5d6eba7b.title: Jeetu Patel: Building Products for the AI Era
adhoc-20261029-5d6eba7b.show_name: A Bit Personal with Jodi Shelton
adhoc-20261029-5d6eba7b.notes:
At 19, Jeetu Patel left Bombay for Chicago with almost nothing: a mother he wouldn’t see again for seven years, a stutter, and no idea whether he’d stay. Today he is President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco, one of the most important technology companies in the world, helping steer it through the AI infrastructure build-out.

In this episode of A Bit Personal, Jodi Shelton sits down with Jeetu for a conversation between new friends, “getting to know each other in public.” He takes us from a community college computer science class to an internship at Doculabs, where he borrowed a quarter million dollars from a mentor to buy into the business and then ran it for 17 years. Then came the move to EMC, the years at Box, and the leap to Cisco six years ago.

Jeetu also opens up about the people who shaped him, including a father whose choices he spent years angry about and eventually forgave, and a mother who was his best friend and whose advice still guides him: take the job that scares you more. We talk about why he never saw his own success as inevitable, what a Taj Mahal tour guide taught him about the power of a platform, and why he believes the most meaningful moments at work come from a team chasing a goal that seems almost impossible.

On the business side, Jeetu explains how Cisco, which missed the cloud wave, is positioning itself as the “picks and shovels” company of the AI gold rush, and how it went from zero to $9.3 billion in AI infrastructure orders from hyperscalers in fiscal 2026. He also makes the case for why AI should be treated as a tool for learning rather than a shortcut around it, why the narrative around the technology needs balance, and why leading in AI is, in his words, “the most American thing we can do.”
We close with the question every executive should be asked: when no one needs anything from you, what does a perfect day look like?
This is a conversation about gratitude, grit, and what you do with the opportunities you’re handed.

adhoc-20261102-79239bab.title: AI Agents, Business Strategy & the Future of Work | Cisco’s Jeetu Patel
adhoc-20261102-79239bab.notes:
How does a global technology company reinvent itself as AI transforms the way businesses operate?

In this conversation from the Digital Leadership Agenda 2027 conference, Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco, joins Vijay Gurbaxani, Director of the Center for Digital Transformation at UC Irvine, to discuss Cisco's transformation, the rise of AI agents, and what business leaders must do to stay competitive.

Patel explains how Cisco is evolving into an integrated technology platform and why the growth of AI is creating new demand for networking, data centers, and security. He also shares how Cisco is adopting AI internally, from introducing AI-powered coding tools to 32,000 engineers to developing AI agents for its 90,000 employees.

The discussion explores why AI transformation is as much a cultural challenge as a technological one. Patel challenges the idea that AI success should be measured primarily through productivity or job cuts, emphasizing the importance of AI fluency, workforce development, and innovation.

As AI agents begin completing tasks independently, Patel and Gurbaxani also examine how these technologies could reshape jobs, business models, and customer relationships.

With AI capabilities advancing, Patel challenges executives to rethink not only how their organizations use technology, but also how they compete in an increasingly agent-driven economy.

adhoc-20261108-826660e1.title: How to Win Deals & Grow a $250B Business | Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto Networks
adhoc-20261108-826660e1.notes:
Nikesh Arora is the chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies. He spent 10 years at Google, where he ran Google Europe and later became chief business officer, as the company grew from about 2,000 to 60,000 employees and from $2 billion to $62 billion in revenue. After two years as president of SoftBank, he joined Palo Alto Networks in 2018, when it was an $18 billion firewall company. Since then it has made about 35 acquisitions and expanded to more than 70 products. Nikesh explains the enterprise economics behind that strategy, why he only buys the number one or number two company in a category, and why he negotiates directly with founders and requires a joint product roadmap before signing a deal. He also tells the story of how he and Egon Durban nearly invested in Oculus before it sold to Facebook, how Egon talked him through a 29-round auction for the London Spirit cricket team, and what it was like selling Google ads when he couldn't tell customers the price or the volume. He also shares the Hindu fatalism that keeps him from worrying about what he can't control, how he approaches parenting, why AI makes cybersecurity more valuable, and why he started posting on X.

a16z-20261109-d464dfe1.title: Scott Kupor on Building a16z and Rebuilding the Federal Workforce
a16z-20261109-d464dfe1.notes: Scott Kupor helped build a16z from three people into a firm with hundreds of employees. Now, as Director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, he’s applying some of the same lessons about talent, incentives, and organizational design to a workforce of roughly two million federal employees. Scott joins Founders host David Senra to tell the story of a16z’s earliest days, from joining Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz during the 2008 financial crisis to borrowing Michael Ovitz’s CAA model to build a venture firm around specialized networks and services for founders. He explains why a16z chose to market itself when venture firms traditionally didn’t, how early wins like Skype accelerated the firm’s growth, and why it eventually reorganized around specialized investing teams. Then they turn to Scott’s move into government. He lays out his effort to build a more merit-based federal workforce, attract younger technical talent, and create what he calls “permissioned risk” so government employees can actually try new things. That includes everything from changing how performance and promotions work to replacing a retirement process that still relied on hundreds of millions of pieces of paper stored in an underground Pennsylvania mine. adhoc-20261110-3a794f35.title: Amazon AWS CEO: AI boom is just getting started
adhoc-20261110-3a794f35.notes:
Amazon thinks its cloud business could generate $1 trillion a year within the next five to ten years. I sit down with AWS CEO Matt Garman in Seattle to understand what gives him that confidence and what could get in the way.

Garman explains how AI is pushing companies to move their core operations into the cloud, accelerating the business AWS spent two decades building. 

We discuss why he thinks inference, the computing required to run AI models, is still below 1 percent of its eventual scale. He says AWS is adding one GPU every 14 seconds and expects capacity shortages for another couple of years. I ask how he decides who gets the GPUs, why he holds capacity back for startups that don’t exist yet, and where he sees risk in the industry’s spending.

Recorded right after the midterm elections, our conversation also covers the backlash against data centers, what the industry needs to do to win over communities, and why he sees deserts as more promising than space.

I also ask about the reset inside Amazon’s Nova team and whether it still intends to compete at the frontier of AI. We get into selling Trainium chips outside AWS, the rise of inference providers like Baseten and Fireworks, and Amazon’s big research bet on using mathematical proofs to help AI agents follow rules.

adhoc-20261109-fab0be26.title: Intel's Earnings Disaster: Bad Luck, Bad Planning, or Both?
adhoc-20261109-fab0be26.notes:
Intel just had its worst day on the stock market in 55 years, with shares falling nearly 30%. But here's the strange part: Intel actually reported a strong quarter. Revenue grew, its data center business surged, and the company beat expectations. So what went wrong?

In this episode of Semi Doped, Vik Sekar and Austin Lyons dig into Intel's Q3 2026 earnings and the problems behind its disappointing outlook.

Three issues are at the center of Intel's troubles: a weakening PC market driven by rising memory prices, a shortage of advanced packaging substrates that limits server CPU production, and a tragic factory accident in Israel that disrupted chiplet supply.

But how much of this was bad luck, and how much was poor planning?

We debate whether Intel should have anticipated the surge in demand for server CPUs from agentic AI, whether its manufacturing strategy can respond quickly enough, and what these problems mean for its ambitions to become a leading-edge foundry alternative to TSMC.

We also step back to examine what Intel's experience tells us about the broader semiconductor market.

Topics covered:

- Why Intel's stock crashed despite strong earnings
- How the AI memory boom is hurting the PC market
- Why substrate shortages are constraining server CPU production
- The consequences of Intel's Fab 28 accident
- Whether Intel misjudged demand for agentic AI CPUs
- Intel 18A, 14A, and the long-term foundry opportunity
- Why strong demand doesn't necessarily translate into revenue
- Why investors are increasingly demanding returns from the AI infrastructure buildout
